survey.structure_call: Split verdict. The process/thread model, timers, IO manager thread layout, signal threads, configuration table and the network hand-off can keep their structure: they are OS threads, queues, condvars and a parameter table, and map onto std::thread, Mutex/Condvar, channels and a declarative macro (or build script) for the 289 parameters, with no need for an async runtime (sql-nio already runs on mio with plain threads). The error convention also keeps its structure mechanically (the OB_FAIL chains become `?`), though error-codes-as-outcomes should become Option/enum. Memory management and the ownership model built on it force a redesign: fallible allocation everywhere (NULL -> OB_ALLOCATE_MEMORY_FAILED, int-returning push_back), polymorphic ObIAllocator where free() may be a no-op, arena-owned object graphs, a thread-local stack of memory contexts driven by macros that write the caller's ret, per-thread THIS_WORKER state, 122 mutable global service slots, locks separate from data, intrusive lists, manual refcounts and a raw-pointer DAG graph. Translating these one-to-one gives unsafe-heavy Rust with raw pointers everywhere; idiomatic Rust needs an explicit context/allocator parameter, arena lifetimes or index-based graphs, Mutex<T>-wrapped state, and a decided OOM policy (fallible try_reserve-style APIs and custom collections for query memory, plus a global allocator that blocks or aborts for everything else). Files that force the call: src/oblib/lib/rc/context.h, src/oblib/lib/allocator/page_arena.h, src/oblib/lib/alloc/ob_malloc_allocator.cpp with src/oblib/lib/resource/ob_resource_mgr.cpp, src/oblib/lib/worker.h, src/share/rc/ob_server_runtime.h, src/data_plane/api/data_plane/scheduler/ob_dag_scheduler.h, src/share/io/ob_io_define.h.
hard_parts: Fallible allocation as the normal path: 4,976 OB_ALLOCATE_MEMORY_FAILED sites and int-returning container ops (src/oblib/lib/container/ob_array.h:304); stable Rust Vec/Box/String abort on OOM and the Allocator trait is nightly-only (assumption from Rust docs), so ports need try_reserve discipline or custom collections such as allocator-api2/hashbrown-style containers.

Memory accounting and limits inside the allocator, with cache eviction on the failure path: src/oblib/lib/resource/ob_resource_mgr.cpp:54-86 and :201-254, src/oblib/lib/alloc/ob_malloc_allocator.cpp; a Rust #[global_allocator] cannot return an error to the caller, only NULL -> handle_alloc_error.

Polymorphic allocator where free() may do nothing and objects are placement-new'd into arenas without destructors: src/oblib/lib/allocator/page_arena.h:975-1029, src/oblib/lib/alloc/ob_iallocator.h; Rust needs arena lifetimes ('a references, bumpalo-style) or indices.
Thread-local memory-context stack and for-loop macros that assign the caller's ret: src/oblib/lib/rc/context.h:46-73, :700-760.

Per-thread worker state reached from anywhere: THIS_WORKER (src/oblib/lib/worker.h, Worker::self_ __thread, 396 uses), ObMallocHookAttrGuard thread-local memory attr (src/oblib/lib/alloc/malloc_hook.cpp:79), ObPageManager::thread_local_instance (src/observer/omt/ob_th_worker.cpp).

Mutable global service slots bound and cleared at runtime: src/share/rc/ob_server_runtime.h:126-148 (122 types, 1,243 call sites); OnceLock does not support unbinding, so this needs explicit context passing or atomic pointer slots.

survey.units_of_work: The natural translation unit is the header/implementation pair: 236 of them across the 93,765 hand-written lines, from git ls-files over the runtime groups with extensions stripped and sort -u. They fall into 14 directory groups that can be ported and tested as units: (1) thread primitives and timers: src/oblib/lib/{thread,thread_local,task}, 44 files; (2) worker runtime and the place where modules are created: src/observer/omt, src/share/{rc,resource}, src/oblib/lib/worker.*; (3) core malloc: src/oblib/lib/alloc; (4) allocator family: src/oblib/lib/allocator, 36 files; (5) object pools: src/oblib/lib/objectpool; (6) locks and queues: src/oblib/lib/{lock,queue}; (7) IO manager: src/share/io; (8) files and local device: src/oblib/lib/{file,restore}, src/share/ob_local_device.*; (9) C++ side of the network hand-off: src/oblib/rpc, src/observer/ob_srv_*, 13 files that call nio_*; (10) DAG scheduler: 12 files; (11) errno: port the generator gen_errno.pl and regenerate from ob_errno.def instead of translating 18,824 generated lines; (12) logging: src/oblib/lib/oblog; (13) signals: 9 files; (14) config and parameters: 25 files plus the 289-entry table. Groups 3, 4 and 2 have to be designed first, because the allocator/OOM policy and how context gets passed determine the signatures of every other unit and of the 2,498 files that use ObIAllocator.
open_questions: Whether the memory limit holds under MALLOC_BACKEND=jemalloc: the jemalloc branch of ObMallocAllocator::realloc skips update_hold. jemalloc hooks or extent limits configured elsewhere were not checked.
How many threads a running server actually has, and of which kinds; this needs a live process (thread list or virtual table), not a read-only look at the source.

Whether the embedded form always runs as a separate server process (run/seekdb.clients, wait_no_client, _Exit in src/observer/ob_server.cpp:1670-1680) or must also load into a host process. This decides whether a Rust port may own signal handlers, the global allocator and panic=abort.
How much vendored C/C++ code (zstd, ICU and others) depends on the glibc malloc hook for memory accounting. A Rust #[global_allocator] does not see C allocations unless the hook is kept.
Which of the 500 tools/obtest tests still run against seekdb, since CI does not use them.

Whether the 206 latch ids and wait-event statistics (ObLatchIds, ObWaitEventIds) are user-visible through virtual tables that tests or users depend on. If so, a Rust Mutex<T> port has to keep that instrumentation.

Whether ReqWorker latency and fairness (100ms poll, adaptive expansion, mclock IO scheduling in src/share/io/io_schedule) can be matched and checked without a benchmark run. This cannot be settled read-only.

verification.size_split_check: Reproduced exactly with the survey's own method: 404 files and 131,046 lines, of which 93,765 hand-written, 31,169 generated, 3,095 data and 3,017 vendored. Every group matches. I also used git grep -c '' to rank files, and that confirmed the generated protobuf/grpc files are the four largest in the network area. The generated/data/vendored classification is sound: 'DO NOT EDIT' appears only in the standbyservice pb files and the errno outputs, and ob_net_easy.cpp is a hand-written replacement for a few libeasy helpers. The split is narrower than the structure call it supports. It leaves out the fallible, allocator-parameterized containers the memory argument rests on: src/oblib/lib/container (32 files, 12,685 lines) and src/oblib/lib/hash (31 files, 14,106). It also leaves out src/share/cache (22 files, 8,356; the KV cache washer and hazard-version reclamation named in hard_parts), src/oblib/lib/stat plus wait_event (16 files, about 3,359; latch ids), src/oblib/lib/utility (45 files, 15,377; includes the OB_FAIL/OB_SUCC macros), and the process entry points src/observer/ob_server.cpp (2,910), main.cpp (889) and src/share/ob_debug_sync.cpp (1,004). If no other area counts these, the runtime is closer to 170k hand-written lines than 94k.
verification.structure_call_check: I agree with the split verdict, with three changes. (1) The memory half still forces a redesign, but for a partly different reason. The survey's central example (ob_malloc returning NULL at a server-wide limit enforced in ObMemoryMgr::update_hold) is not the default runtime. Linux and macOS builds default to jemalloc (CMakeLists.txt:213-214, deps/external/CMakeLists.txt:17-19, ob_malloc.cpp:147-151), and there ob_malloc/ObMallocAllocator/the malloc hook call je_malloc directly with no limit check (ob_malloc.h:118-125, ob_malloc_allocator.cpp:67-70, malloc_hook.cpp:163-164). What stays is the int/NULL-return convention at about 5k sites, module budgets that return NULL (ob_block_alloc_mgr.h:38-49; memstore, KV cache and vector limits from commit 38bd9c622), polymorphic ObIAllocator with no-op free (page_arena.h:1020), the thread-local context stack with ret-writing macros (context.h:65-67), intrusive lists and manual refcounts. Those still rule out an idiomatic one-to-one translation. But it means a Rust port can do what the C++ already does: jemalloc as the global allocator, aborting on true OOM, with budgets as explicit fallible allocator objects only where query memory is bounded. That is less work than the 'fallible everywhere' reading suggests. (2) The thread side keeps its structure more easily than the hard parts imply. Custom mmap'd stacks are used only on Linux (thread.cpp:84-118); macOS, Android and Windows already use pthread_attr_setstacksize, which std::thread::Builder::stack_size covers. (3) The thread/timer side has more mechanisms than the survey names: ObTimeWheel, ObDedupQueue, ObUniqTaskQueue, ObAsyncTaskQueue, ObDynamicThreadPool, ObMapQueueThreadPool, ObOccamThreadPool, ObLightyQueue, and ObIndependentDag run by ObDDLDagThreadPool (src/storage/ddl/ob_ddl_dag_thread_pool.h:29). They can keep their shape, but a port should merge them into a few Rust primitives rather than translate each one. The signal half is smaller than stated because do_with_crash_restore is dead code, so siglongjmp is only in memory_dump.cpp. The network hand-off, errno table and parameter table keep their structure as the survey says.

missed.point: The default allocator backend is jemalloc, and on that path the process-wide memory limit and KV-cache washing are not enforced. Memory limits now live in per-module budgets. This changes the OOM-policy analysis the survey builds its redesign case on, and it answers the survey's open question 1: the limit does not hold under jemalloc.

missed.point: On Linux, Rust code in the process already allocates through the C++ malloc override. The 'which global allocator' question for a mixed C++/Rust period is therefore already settled by the hook. Under jemalloc, a NULL reaches Rust's handle_alloc_error and aborts; under obmalloc, the hook retries forever. A Rust port that installs its own #[global_allocator] must keep the hook or remove it.
missed.evidence: malloc_hook.cpp overrides malloc/free/realloc/memalign/malloc_usable_size, and malloc_hook_extended.cpp:72-195 overrides calloc/aligned_alloc/posix_memalign/valloc/pvalloc. src/observer/CMakeLists.txt links sql_nio and malloc_hook into seekdb (lines 20, 36, 51, 97, 103). git grep global_allocator over rust/ = 0 hits.

verification.overall: For raw counts and code structure, the survey can be trusted. Almost every count reproduced exactly, or within a few percent, with a different method (line and distinct-file counts instead of -c sums, a Perl pass instead of awk, a function list pulled from nio.h). Every cited path and line number I opened says what the survey claims, and the six bug-fix commits exist with the stated contents. Its weak spot is the memory section, which matters most for the decision. It presents the obmalloc path (server hard limit, KV-cache washing, a malloc hook that retries forever) as how the server behaves, but Linux and macOS builds default to jemalloc, where none of that runs and limits are per-module budgets. The redesign verdict for memory still holds because of the int/NULL-return convention, arenas, context macros and intrusive structures, but the reasoning and the proposed OOM policy have to be restated from the jemalloc default. Smaller problems: several counts come from loose regexes (nio_* calls 61 vs 37, O_DIRECT 76 vs 54, lock declarations 546 vs about 460, context macros 175 vs about 49 ret-writing uses); the CI test count is 272, not 283, and two cited example tests are not run; the sql-nio 'already fails softly' claim is overstated; do_with_crash_restore is dead code; and the size split leaves out containers, hash and the KV cache that the argument depends on. Two open questions can be settled from the source. The embedded mode is a flag on the seekdb executable (ob_command_line_parser.cpp:364; the only shared library, liboceanbase.so, is a Linux pretest target), and latch ids are no longer user-visible. Use the survey's numbers and structure description as they are, but re-derive the allocator/OOM section before it feeds the migration decision.

critic.coverage: The fifteen areas cover every top-level module under src/ (sql 983,706 lines, storage 760,249, oblib 382,226, share 271,801, observer 132,632, rootserver 104,311, pl 42,811, logservice 32,705, query 30,639, data_plane 16,157, standby 14,899, objit 2,486; HEAD 076eb309b). They also cover the cross-cutting questions: idioms, coupling, runtime, deps, build, pain and the test judge. The structure call is well supported: every core area independently finds that ownership and memory need a redesign while the outer code can be translated file by file, and the verifiers mostly corrected numbers rather than conclusions. Five things are still weak. (1) Some claims conflict and nobody has settled them. On data compatibility, storage says there is no such constraint, tx-log says v1.4.0 is the baseline, and tests-judge says the binary refuses other versions. I checked: src/oblib/common/ob_data_version_mgr.cpp:61 returns OB_NOT_SUPPORTED when the persisted data version differs from DATA_CURRENT_VERSION, a check added on 2026-07-26/27. On memory, oblib, idioms and pain treat out-of-memory as a recoverable error, but the runtime verifier found that jemalloc is the default backend. I also found no mysqltest .result file that expects -4013/HY001. (2) The verification cost has no Rust-side scaling assumption, and the digests do not include the C++ clean-build baseline. (3) Nobody has measured which of the planned units the 272 CI cases actually reach, beyond expression function names. (4) Sizes overlap between areas (share/geo, observer/vector_index, the storage vector and retrieval directories). About 45K lines belong to no area: sql/engine/cmd, sql/monitor, sql/privilege_check, sql/executor, observer/change_stream, observer/dbms_scheduler, rootserver/dbms_job, and the AI-service code. Nobody gave token sizes per unit, and the model plan needs them. (5) Nobody measured things outside the source tree that bear on the verdict. The tree changes fast: 504 commits and +2.2M/-3.9M lines in src/ over the last 90 days, 151 of those commits by the 'obdev' mirror account. Test assets sit in sibling repos: seekdb-bindings lib/tests and python/tests, seekdb-async/tests, shell-e2e, and unittest/wasm on the wasm branch. The wasm32 branch is live: 366 files changed.

gaps.why: Four areas disagree on whether a Rust seekdb must read data written by the C++ build. storage-core says it is not a constraint. tx-log proposes a v1.4.0 baseline, but its verifier found that v1.4.0 is not an ancestor of HEAD. tests-judge says the server refuses any data version other than its own. search-vector-gis and deps make vsag snapshots, S2 cell ids and FTS tokens conditional on this answer. It decides whether storage, clog, OB_UNIS, ObNumber, CRC and the vsag/S2 formats must stay byte-exact, or whether they can be redesigned. It is also the strongest candidate for the fact that would change the verdict.

Nobody knows which of the planned units (61 operators, 528 expression types, about 93 statement resolvers, 34 rewrite rules, 146 virtual tables, the DDL kinds) any case reaches. So the report cannot size 'build the judge first' or sketch parity scenarios per unit. Differential runs against the C++ binary also need to know whether any output order depends on pointer addresses, which would make EXPLAIN differ even when the logic is identical.

gaps.why: A verdict of 'now' versus 'later' depends on how fast the C++ tree changes and on where changes come from. The tree had 504 commits and +2.2M/-3.9M lines in src/ in the last 90 days, from at least 12 authors. 151 of those commits are by 'obdev', the internal mirror, and tx-log notes the pruning is still going on. If seekdb still takes fixes from OceanBase mainline, a Rust rewrite cuts off that stream, which is an ongoing cost no area weighed. Parallel feature lines, such as feature/webassembly-shell, would also have to be re-ported.

gaps.why: oblib, idioms, pain and runtime all build part of the redesign case, and a large rulebook cost, on 'out-of-memory is a recoverable error': 4,976 OB_ALLOCATE_MEMORY_FAILED sites and 6,302 OB_FAIL(push_back) calls, which would need fallible collections everywhere. The runtime verifier found that jemalloc is the default backend (ob_malloc.cpp parse_ob_malloc_backend) and that the global limit and KV-cache washing do not run on that path. I found no mysqltest .result that expects -4013/HY001. If only a few module budgets can actually fail, the Rust rulebook could accept abort-on-OOM plus budget checks, which removes a whole class of translation work. This must be settled before the rulebook is drafted.
gaps.brief: Read-only in /Users/colin/seekdb-dev/migrate-to-rust. (1) Under the default backend (OB_HAVE_BUNDLED_JEMALLOC, src/oblib/lib/allocator/ob_malloc.cpp:143-160), trace every path by which an allocation can return NULL or fail to a caller: ObMallocAllocator ctx and label limits on the jemalloc path (ob_malloc_allocator.cpp), the module budgets in ob_block_alloc_mgr.h:38-49 and their 14 users, ObArenaAllocator/PageArena limits, ObSqlMemMgrProcessor (does it spill or fail?), the memstore throttle in storage/throttle, and the memory_limit/system_memory parameters in ob_parameter_seed.ipp. Give file:line for each. (2) Estimate which of the OB_ALLOCATE_MEMORY_FAILED sites sit behind an allocator that can really fail in the default build, and which only check a jemalloc NULL that in practice never comes back. (3) Check the public surface. Does any .result file, init.sql or init_user.sql, or any seekdb-bindings test (/Users/colin/seekdb-dev/seekdb-bindings/lib/tests, python/tests) expect error 4013 or HY001, or set a memory limit low enough to trigger it? (4) Check how rust/sql-nio handles allocation failure today (try_reserve uses and #[global_allocator]), and whether the malloc hook sends Rust allocations through jemalloc on Linux and macOS. Output: a list of real fail points, and a recommendation between 'fallible collections everywhere' and 'abort on OOM plus explicit budget checks at N named sites'.

survey.what_it_is: The startup check that decides whether a seekdb binary will open an existing data directory: src/oblib/common/ob_data_version_mgr.{h,cpp} compares etc/seekdb.data_version.bin with DATA_CURRENT_VERSION (src/oblib/common/ob_version_def.h:53). Around it sits everything else the server persists, which this survey checks against that gate, against the v1.4.0 release, and against any promise of upgrade or logical export.

survey.summary:
The gate is real and strict. validate_or_init_current_version returns OB_NOT_SUPPORTED when the stored version is not exactly DATA_CURRENT_VERSION (1.4.0.0). load_from_file also rejects the 1.3.0-era file layout (header version 1 vs 2). It runs in ObServer::init → init_config, before IO, storage, super block, slog replay, clog and tablet load, so on a mismatch no sstable, slog or clog byte is parsed. It has three gaps. SQLite meta.db is opened, __all_sys_parameter is created if missing and all parameters are loaded before the check. A missing version file is taken as a fresh install without checking whether store/ or clog already hold data. And the check compares only a constant that did not change when formats did. v1.4.0 has the identical gate and the same 1.4.0.0 value. It is not an ancestor of HEAD, but it is the master merge-base 977053bf1 plus one deps-only commit. After that point, slog sub-types 2/3/4/9/10/11/13 and the DDL clog types 0x20/0x40 were removed (da23ae158, d51422b54) without a version bump, so "same data version" does not mean "same bytes". The core headers (palf, tx log, micro block, TableType, ObCompressorType, record header, tablet meta header) have zero source diff between v1.4.0 and HEAD. The project has already dropped in-place upgrade on its own: the upgrade machinery was deleted in 3609383cd (2026-06-26), 1.4.0 refuses 1.3.0 data, standby restore requires equal versions, and no doc, README, release note, package hook or binding promises data migration. The package hooks only carry seekdb.cnf across an upgrade, and the bindings return a generic SEEKDB_INTERNAL_ERROR. The derived artifacts (vsag snapshots, S2 cell ids, FTS token rows) are rows inside gated storage whose bytes come from outside libraries or tokenizers with no version tag. All of them can be rebuilt through SQL (DROP/CREATE INDEX, DBMS_VECTOR.REBUILD_INDEX). A logical export/import path exists (SELECT INTO OUTFILE, LOAD DATA, LOCK/UNLOCK TABLES accepted as no-ops for mysqldump), but public tests barely cover it: 0 OUTFILE tests, 1 LOAD DATA test, 0 mysqldump tests, 0 restart tests.

survey.structure_call: The gate itself is small (4 files, 730 lines of plain file I/O and a comparison) and translates one-to-one into idiomatic Rust (std::fs plus a parsed struct). What matters for the whole migration is what it allows. Because the binary already refuses any other data version before storage, slog or clog are parsed, the Rust build can bump DATA_CURRENT_VERSION and redesign the on-disk formats (storage blocks, clog/palf, OB_UNIS field orders, ObNumber and CRC encodings) instead of copying them byte for byte. Three conditions: move the check ahead of the meta.db open, or keep meta.db as plain SQLite, which is free with rusqlite; close the missing-file hole; and keep behavior (not bytes) equal for vsag, S2 and tokenizer output so query results match. Files that force the call: src/oblib/common/ob_data_version_mgr.cpp:50-70, src/oblib/common/ob_version_def.h:53, src/observer/ob_server.cpp:1698-1719.
hard_parts: Startup order: meta.db (SQLite) is opened, its table is created and every parameter is read before the version check (src/observer/ob_server.cpp:1698-1719; src/share/config/ob_config_storage.cpp:47-85). A Rust build that changes the SQLite schema has to move the check first or migrate the schema in SQL.

Missing-version-file hole: ENOENT is treated as a fresh install and nothing is cross-checked against existing store/ or clog data (src/oblib/common/ob_data_version_mgr.cpp:58-60, 88-94; ob_server.cpp:410-433 runs later). A Rust cutover must close this or old C++ data directories would slip past the check.

Same version, different bytes: slog sub-types and DDL clog types were removed after v1.4.0 without a bump (da23ae158, d51422b54). Any byte-compatibility target would have to name a commit, not a version, and would need golden data directories written by that commit.

If byte compatibility were kept, some serializers copy whole C++ structs with MEMCPY, so the format is whatever compiler layout and padding happen to be: src/storage/ob_super_block_struct.cpp:60,72; src/storage/blocksstable/ob_simplified_sstable_macro_block_header.cpp:99,113; src/storage/memtable/ob_memtable_mutator.cpp:110-137. Rust would need #[repr(C)] mirrors with the exact padding.

The serialization byte contract is spread across macro field lists in .cpp files. Macro counts per directory: src/storage 102 OB_SERIALIZE_MEMBER* / 140 OB_UNIS_VERSION*, src/share 201/251, src/sql 304/396, src/oblib 33/41, src/standby 20/20. Not all are persisted; the sql ones are mostly in-process plans.

vsag snapshots are streamed through C++ std::streambuf subclasses with callbacks (src/observer/vector_index/ob_plugin_vector_index_serialize.cpp:31-240) into vsag's Serialize(std::ostream&) (src/oblib/lib/vector/ob_vsag_adaptor.cpp:1276,1338). Rust needs a C++ shim for as long as vsag is the library.

Derived-data behavior must stay equal even without byte compatibility: S2 coverings come from C++ s2geometry 0.10.0 (src/share/geo/ob_s2adapter.cpp), and FTS words from the IK tokenizer and 276,043-line dictionary (src/storage/fts/dict/ob_ik_dic.cpp). A Rust S2 or tokenizer that differs changes query results in the 16 spatial and 24 fulltext mysqltest files.
pain_instances: src/storage/ob_super_block_struct.cpp:60,72 serialize and deserialize ObServerSuperBlockHeader with MEMCPY(this) / MEMCPY(this, buf), so the on-disk layout is whatever the C++ compiler lays out; Rust would force an explicit encoding.
src/storage/memtable/ob_memtable_mutator.cpp:126-137 copies MEMCPY(this, buf + pos, min(sizeof(*this), meta_size_)), defensive partial copying of a struct to survive size changes between versions.

src/oblib/common/ob_data_version_mgr.cpp:170-175 and 257-258 place ObDataVersion into an arena with placement new and never destroy it; lines 241-252 parse the file with STRTOK_R and sscanf into fixed char buffers ('%63s %lu %c', ob_data_version_mgr.h:66-69). This is hand-written defensive C-string parsing that owned Rust types and str parsing remove.
survey.public_surface_tests: The gate and persistence across restart: 0 public-surface tests. No mysqltest file restarts the server (git grep for restart/shutdown_server in tools/deploy/mysql_test/*.test = 0), and CI (.github/workflows/seekdb.yml) runs only mysqltest slices. The only test mentioning data_version is the legacy OceanBase obtest tools/obtest/t/rootservice/zhoulan_dataversion_reboot.test (cluster bootstrap, not the seekdb gate). Logical export/import: SELECT INTO OUTFILE 0 files; LOAD DATA 1 file (test_suite/fts_index/t/load_data.test); mysqldump 0; SHOW CREATE TABLE 34 files. Rebuild paths for derived data: DBMS_VECTOR rebuild_index 8 files (e.g. test_suite/vector_index/t/rebuild_vector_index.test, fork_table/t/fork_table_vector.test); fulltext 24, spatial index 16 and vector index 24 .test files check tokenizer, S2 and vsag behavior through query results, not on-disk bytes. All counts: git grep -l -i <pattern> -- 'tools/deploy/mysql_test/*.test' | wc -l. These tests use only SQL, so they survive a Rust rewrite unchanged; none of them would catch a persistence regression.
survey.units_of_work: Without byte compatibility, which the evidence supports: (1) the gate, 1 unit (ob_data_version_mgr.{h,cpp} + ob_version_def.{h,cpp}, 4 files, 730 lines), translated directly, plus fixing the meta.db-first order and the missing-file hole; (2) a new cutover unit that is not a translation: a tested logical export/import path (OUTFILE/LOAD DATA/mysqldump round-trip over every column type, index kind and generated column); (3) three units where behavior must stay equal: vsag adaptor and snapshot stream (3 files, 1,980 lines, likely kept as FFI to C++ vsag), S2 adapter (4 files, 1,343 lines, FFI or a verified port), FTS tokenizers (71 files, 10,526 lines, plus the 276,043-line dictionary data). With byte compatibility, add one codec unit per format family, each needing golden data directories from a named C++ commit: palf headers (8 files), slog + slog_ckpt (48 files), tx log (2 files), super block + runtime meta (4 files), SQLite meta.db storage (17 files), plus the sstable/tablet codecs owned by the storage areas.
open_questions: Whether a real v1.4.0 data directory actually starts on HEAD: it passes the gate (same 1.4.0.0), but it depends on whether v1.4.0's bootstrap checkpoint already truncated the now-removed slog sub-types (2,3,4,9,10,11,13) and DDL clog types (0x20/0x40), and on whether the persisted create_status value equals 1. This needs a runtime test.

Whether 'refuse any other data version' is a product decision or a side effect of the 2026-07 cleanup commits. There is no release note or doc, and embedded/pip users would only see SEEKDB_INTERNAL_ERROR after an upgrade.

Whether SELECT INTO OUTFILE + LOAD DATA, or mysqldump, round-trips every seekdb type and DDL feature (VECTOR, GEOMETRY/SRID, JSON, LOBs, generated columns, fulltext/vector/spatial index DDL, sys packages). The public tests do not check this.

Whether packaging still builds at HEAD: cmake/RPM.cmake, cmake/DEB.cmake and package/deb/seekdb-build.sh reference tools/systemd templates deleted in 45cbbe9e1. Bazel packaging may have replaced this path; this could not be checked read-only.
Whether meta.db content other than parameters (__all_tablet_meta_table, checksums, merge info) must survive a cutover or can be regenerated.

If the migration ships intermediate releases that mix C++ and Rust modules in one binary, those modules must share one on-disk format inside a release. That is a separate constraint from reading older releases' data, and depends on how the work is split.

verification.structure_call_check: I agree with the direction, with caveats. The gate is small, plain file I/O (ob_data_version_mgr.cpp: open, read, ObRecordHeader, STRTOK_R/sscanf at 249/252, placement new at 175/275; the survey cites 257-258, which is off). It maps directly to Rust std::fs plus a parsed struct. The code already has no multi-version reader: besides the gate (ob_data_version_mgr.cpp:61), strict DATA_CURRENT_VERSION equality is enforced in ob_medium_compaction_info.cpp:330/438, ob_trans_service_v4.cpp:93, ob_tx_table_define.cpp:86, ob_macro_block_meta.cpp:204/223/471/499/542 and ob_pl_user_type.cpp:422. So bumping the version and redesigning formats matches how the project already works; 1.4.0 already refuses 1.3.0 data. The caveats are stronger than the survey says. (1) The missing-file hole is not only hypothetical. v1.0.0/v1.0.1 wrote etc/observer.data_version.bin (v1.0.1:deps/oblib/src/common/ob_tenant_data_version_mgr.h:162, renamed in 581c57990). At HEAD, such a directory takes the fresh-install branch (ob_data_version_mgr.cpp:88-94, 58-60), and check_need_initialize (ob_server.cpp:410-433) sets need_initialize=false because block_file and clog exist, so storage parsing starts. (2) meta.db holds more than parameters, for example the standby role state saved as a config value (src/standby/control/standby_state_store.cpp:172-205), and it is opened before the gate (ob_server.cpp:1713-1715). (3) The 'no byte compatibility' freedom applies between releases, not inside one. If the port ships mixed C++/Rust binaries, the slog, clog and sstable codecs on each side of a boundary must agree byte for byte in that release. (4) The export must run on the old C++ binary, and the installers restart the new binary straight away (tools/macpkg/launchd/profile/postinstall), so the safety of the cutover depends on code that has already shipped.

It is not only a theoretical cutover risk.

verification.overall: The survey can be trusted to a high degree. I reproduced every count: file and line totals, commit ancestry (692/1, merge-base 977053bf1), the zero-diff list of persisted-format headers, the test counts and the macro counts. Every behavior claim about the gate, its startup order, the meta.db exception, the missing-file hole, the slog and DDL-clog removals, the runtime-meta legacy field, standby restore, bindings and packaging matches the code. The only errors are small line offsets (1134 vs 1135; main.cpp 808/820-822 vs 809/823; 257-258 vs 272-275). C13 and C23 needed factual corrections. C13 overstates 'never a seekdb 1.x upgrade chain': v1.1.0 still carried OceanBase compatible-version scaffolding for 1.0.x/1.1.0. C23 counts the #define as a use. The public_surface_tests text wrongly says only one obtest file mentions data_version, and it ignores the in-tree obtest reboot harness. The main weakness is in the assessment, not the facts. The survey treats the missing-file hole as a cutover risk, but it already applies to v1.0.0/v1.0.1 directories. It does not see that strict version equality is also built into persisted objects, which supports its own conclusion. It does not note that same-version byte drift can hang DDL clog replay instead of failing. And it understates that 'not required' covers reading older releases only: mixed C++/Rust releases still need byte agreement, and the export depends on C++ code that has already shipped. With those caveats, its one-line conclusion stands: byte compatibility is not required; a version bump plus logical export is enough.

survey.summary:
The judge reaches far less than the unit counts suggest, and a read-only pass can only bound that reach.
- **Operators:** 40 of the 272 configured .result files carry EXPLAIN tables; the figure of 42 counted two a_trade files whose column names start with OPERATOR_. Those 658 plan tables show 36 of the 61 registered physical operator types. Statement shapes suggest 4 more are executed (REPLACE, ON DUPLICATE KEY, window functions, and the VALUES operator under every EXPLAIN). 8 more are plausible but unproven, and 13 have no evidence at all, including recursive CTE, SAMPLE, SELECT INTO, JSON_TABLE, join filter and stats gathering.
- **Statements:** 44 of 89 resolver classes are reached. Of the 45 unreached, 5 cannot be produced by either grammar, and 2 (CreatePackage and CreatePackageBody) are hit only when system packages load at startup.
- **Expressions:** 207 of 527 registered names show any evidence. Array/map (4 of 35), JSON (6 of 33), date/time (14 of 62) and vector index internals are largely unreached; names such as hour(, month( and unix_timestamp( appear in none of the 283 .test files.
- **Rewrite rules:** only 9 of 34 show their effect in any plan or outline, one more is named only by a NO_UNNEST hint, and 24 show nothing.
- **init.sql gate:** init.sql matters more than its 54 lines suggest. It turns on recyclebin, which is off by default, so every DROP goes through the recycle bin. Its 12 set_tp lines switch on self-checks read through OB_E, which is compiled into release builds too: EXPLAIN plans are regenerated from their own outline, rewrite convergence and expression formalization are checked, the new sort path is forced, NLJ/SPF batches are forced to group size 4, and the fast NLJ range generator is cross-checked. One tracepoint (509) has no reader at all.
- **Coverage:** a measured coverage run is close to ready. The clang source-based flags (cmake/Env.cmake:67-74) and the constructor that writes the profraw file (src/observer/main.cpp:19) still exist. Only the Bazel migration commit 4cb6fb268 blocks them (CMakeLists.txt:147 FATAL_ERROR, build.sh:241), so a one-day measured check is realistic.
- **Pointer-address order:** I found no sort or hash iteration keyed by pointer value whose order reaches EXPLAIN text or result rows. Every pointer-keyed map in these directories is lookup-only, feeds another map, or is dead code.
- **What does bind a port:** the judge compares exact text. That text includes 568 plan tables with floating-point EST.ROWS/EST.TIME, query-block names printed as %08X hashes, std::sort tie order, 2,688 expected-error directives, and 10,107 of 11,908 SELECT...FROM statements with no ORDER BY, which depend on C++ hash-table output order. Those, not pointer addresses, constrain how a port may be structured.

survey.structure_call:
**The registries:** these translate one-to-one into Rust enums with match tables. That covers the REGISTER_OPERATOR macro table (61 entries), the REG_OP list (526 classes), the resolver switch (89 classes, 5 of them dead) and the fixed 34-rule list. Their current C++ form (macro-generated template traits, placement new, dynamic_cast checks) is a mechanism Rust replaces rather than something to preserve.

**What the judge forces:** the judge compares exact text, and that forces structure-preserving translation, or a relaxed judge, for the parts that produce the text:
- the cost model and filter ranking behind 568 plan tables with EST.ROWS/EST.TIME
- the %08X query-block-name hash in outline data
- std::sort tie order wherever ties can reach output
- the C++ hash-table output order behind 10,107 SELECTs with no ORDER BY
- the OB_E self-check hooks that init.sql turns on.

A redesign of the optimizer or of hash execution would fail the current judge unless plans and rows are first normalized.

Files that force the call: src/sql/optimizer/ob_logical_operator.cpp, src/sql/optimizer/ob_log_join.cpp, src/sql/resolver/dml/ob_sql_hint.cpp, src/oblib/lib/utility/ob_sort.h, src/sql/optimizer/ob_explain_log_plan.cpp, and the 40 plan-bearing .result files under tools/deploy/mysql_test.
hard_parts: Operator registration built from macros and template specializations: src/query/api/query/engine/ob_operator_reg.h:68-100 (REGISTER_OPERATOR counts its arguments and generates ObOpTypeTraits<N> specializations at :75), with a table filled at static-init time in src/sql/engine/ob_operator_factory.cpp:305-334.

Spec and operator objects are placement-new'd after a 16-byte-aligned child-pointer array in the same allocation, with a manual destructor call and free on failure: src/sql/engine/ob_operator_factory.cpp:187-212 and :219-252. In Rust this needs an arena plus indices, or a separate Vec of children.

Code generation downcasts ObLogicalOperator to the registered logical class with dynamic_cast and reports a mismatch at runtime: src/sql/engine/ob_operator_factory.cpp:278-300. This is inheritance-based dispatch that a Rust enum turns into a compile-time check.

The expression registry builds a throwaway object in a lambda to read its name and type into global NAME_TYPES/OP_ALLOC arrays: src/sql/engine/expr/ob_expr_operator_factory.cpp:431-445, 528 REG_OP lines covering 526 classes.

Pointer identity used as a hash input and map key during expression dedup, copy and replace: src/sql/resolver/expr/ob_shared_expr_resolver.cpp:67-87 ((uintptr_t) of child exprs), src/sql/resolver/expr/ob_raw_expr_copier.cpp:112-207, src/sql/resolver/expr/ob_raw_expr_replacer.cpp:335-465. survey.public_surface_tests:
The 272 configured cases are the public-surface tests for this area: SQL scripts over the MySQL protocol, with no internal imports.
- **Size:** 38,763 statements parsed from 91,961 .test lines plus sourced .inc files, checked against 912,659 lines of recorded .result output.
- **Resolvers:** reached across 248 cases (Select), 226 (Insert), 250 (CreateTable), 72 (CreateIndex), 40 (AlterTable, 319 statements) and 40 (Explain, 409 statements).
- **Plan checks:** concentrated in executor.basic (152 plan tables), subquery.subquery (42), vector_index.sparse_vector_index_vsag_query (41), fts_index.simple_query (39), geometry.geometry_filter_mysql (39), dist_nest_loop_simple (38), executor.full_join (36) and topk (28).
- **Expressions:** exercised mainly by the geometry suite (47 of 65 GIS names), expr.*, type_date.*, vector_index.* and ai_function.ai_prompt.
- **Setup:** init.sql and init_user.sql run before the cases and change behaviour for all of them: recyclebin on, 12 tracepoint self-checks, 6 parameters.
- **Not configured:** tools/obtest/t holds 500 more .test files in a separate harness, and 11 tracked mysql_test cases are left out of the config.

The init.sql gate in each family:

- **Resolvers:** Deallocate and GetDiagnostics appear only inside init.sql's uncalled exec_sql body.

verification.structure_call_check: I partly agree. The registries do map one-to-one onto Rust enums with match tables: 61 REGISTER_OPERATOR lines in ob_operator_reg.h, filled at static-init time and dispatched through dynamic_cast checks in ob_operator_factory.cpp:187-300; 528 REG_OP lines for 526 classes in ob_expr_operator_factory.cpp; the resolver switch in ob_resolver.cpp (89 classes, 5 unreachable from the grammar); and the fixed 33+1 rule list at ob_transformer_impl.cpp:455-487. PHY_TABLE_ROW_STORE and PHY_MULTI_PART_TABLE_SCAN can be dropped. I also agree that the exact-text judge forces structure-preserving translation, or a normalized judge, for the parts that produce text. The survey weights those parts wrongly, though. (1) std::sort tie order barely matters inside the optimizer. reorder_filters_exprs breaks ties by original_pos (ob_logical_operator.h:305-313), and print_join_tables_in_hint sorts by name. The tie-order risk that matters is in result rows from the SORT operator: OB's own ObAdaptiveQS/radix sort and std::sort in ob_sort_op_impl.cpp, with init.sql tracepoint 1200 forcing which path runs (ob_optimizer_util.cpp:6989). (2) Most unordered SELECTs are single-table shapes, about 7,500 of about 10,060. Their order comes from storage and PX scan order, not hash tables, so the hash-function constraint covers only about 300 statements. (3) The plan tables also bind layers outside the optimizer. EST.ROWS comes from storage estimation (ob_access_path_estimation.cpp:165/569 into src/storage/access/ob_table_estimator.cpp and ob_index_sstable_estimator.cpp). The Outputs & filters blocks print expression trees with implicit casts (369 'cast(' output lines) and internal names (495 lines with T_FUN_/T_OP_/column_conv/lnnvl), which binds type deduction and the expression printer. (4) Only 40 cases carry plan tables. So masking EST.ROWS/EST.TIME and rowset= in those 40 files is cheap, and would free the cost model far more than the survey implies. Everything else in the survey's forcing list stands: the %08X qb-name hash at ob_sql_hint.cpp:389, the OB_E hooks, and the 568 cost-bearing tables.

missed.point: How the runner behaves shapes any differential judge. Cases are split into 4 slices; each slice runs its share of the config list in order on one shared instance, and a failing case is retried up to 3 times on a freshly destroyed, restarted and init.sql-seeded instance. So a case passes if any of 4 attempts pass, which hides flakiness. Global state also leaks from case to case within a slice: alter system parameters such as vector_memory_limit, debug_sync_timeout and the merge intervals, and recycle bin contents.
missed.evidence: .github/script/seekdb/mysqltest_for_seekdb.py:19 (MAX_CASE_RETRIES = 3), :490-518 (the slice_index::slice_count selection, the retry loop, and prepare_instance after a failure), :157-194 (prepare_instance = destroy + start + wait-ready + execute_init_sql). .github/workflows/seekdb.yml:25 sets MYSQLTEST_SLICES to 4. Comparison is plain mysqltest --result-file with no extra normalization (:326-340).

missed.point: Tests depend on named debug-sync points and on tracepoints beyond init.sql. DEBUG_SYNC is live in release builds. Seven configured cases drive named sync points inside DDL and storage code, and three cases set tracepoint 368 themselves. A port must keep these points, with the same names, at equivalent places, or these cases hang or fail. The survey covered only init.sql's tracepoints.
missed.evidence: src/share/ob_debug_sync.h:225-226 ('TODO baihua: empty macro for release version?', #define DEBUG_SYNC(sync_point) GDS.execute(...)). ob_global_debug_sync values in the tests: FORK_TABLE_BUILD_DATA 46 uses, FORK_TABLE_WAIT_DATA_COMPLEMENT 6, FORK_TABLE_SUCCESS 4, REBUILD_VEC_INDEX_* 5, BEFORE_TABLET_FULL_DIRECT_LOAD_MGR_CLOSE 2, CREATE_INDEX_REPLICA_BUILD 1, in fork_table.fork_table_{chain,cow,ddl,lock,merge,with_index} and vector_index.rebuild_vector_index. set_tp 368 appears at histogram/t/stats_farm.test:13/180 and vector_calc_{gbk,utf8}_mysql.test:8.

missed.point: EST.ROWS in the 568 cost-bearing plan tables comes partly from the storage layer's row estimation, not only from the optimizer's cost model. Plan-text parity therefore binds the storage estimators and memtable-vs-sstable state, which the tests steer with major/minor freezes and merge waits. Structure-preserving translation cannot stop at src/sql/optimizer.
missed.evidence: src/sql/optimizer/ob_access_path_estimation.cpp:165 and :569-669 (process_storage_estimation, add_storage_estimation_task[_by_ranges]); the estimators are in src/storage/access/ob_table_estimator.cpp and src/storage/access/ob_index_sstable_estimator.cpp. Tests force merges through mysql_test/include/index_quick_major.inc and wait_daily_merge.inc, sourced by a_trade_notify, bulk_insert, index_14_hint, two_order_by and others. The survey's own EN_THROW_DS_ERROR reader (ob_access_path_estimation.cpp:1765) sits on this path.

missed.point: For ORDER BY rows with equal keys, the output order is set by the SORT operator's own algorithms, not by any address. It is OB's adaptive quicksort/radix on encoded keys or std::sort with the row comparator, chosen by optimizer heuristics that init.sql tracepoint 1200 overrides. libc++ and libstdc++ implement std::sort differently, which is one likely source of the macOS/Linux baseline drift. A Rust port must reproduce these exact algorithms, or the judge must sort ties.
missed.evidence: src/sql/engine/sort/ob_sort_op_impl.cpp:77-260 (ObAdaptiveQS, aqs_radix, inplace_radixsort_more_bucket), :1459/:1462/:1862 (lib::ob_sort over rows with CopyableComparer); src/oblib/lib/utility/ob_sort.h:40 (std::sort); src/sql/optimizer/ob_optimizer_util.cpp:6967-6991 (the can_sort_opt heuristics, overridden when EN_ENABLE_NEWSORT_FORCE is set).

missed.point: The plan text binds the expression printer and implicit-cast insertion, not just operator names. 'Outputs & filters' prints full expression trees with inserted casts, internal function names and batch sizes. Matching them needs the same type deduction, cast placement and printer format.
missed.evidence: Across tracked results there are 4,005 '<n> - output(' lines. 369 contain 'cast(' and 495 contain T_FUN_/T_OP_/column_conv/lnnvl. rowset=16 appears 3,035 times and rowset=256 563 times (from ObCodeGenerator::detect_batch_size, called at ob_explain_log_plan.cpp:56). Example: subquery/r/mysql/subquery.result:441 filter([lnnvl(cast(t1.c2 = 5, TINYINT(-1, 0)))]).

verification.overall: For raw counts and code paths the survey holds up well. I reproduced the configured-case set, the 658 plan tables and their 36/61 operator mapping, and the dead operator paths. The resolver registry arithmetic and the unreached resolvers also check out, as do the init.sql tracepoint readers and their release-build activity, the coverage switches and the commits that blocked them, and the finding that no pointer-keyed ordering reaches output. Several secondary claims are wrong or overstated, though. Only 4 parameters are init.sql-only, not 6, and tests set 12 parameters, not 9. The inner-table case counts include commented-out lines (__all_table is in 24 cases, not 41). Plan tables come from 10 of 27 suite groups, not 16 of 28. The two ob_item_type.h copies differ in real enum members, not just comments. FASTMINMAX and JOIN_LIMIT_PUSHDOWN visibly fire, so the rewrite-rule reach of 9 is a lower bound. Not all drops go through the recycle bin. The survey also misattributes the order risk: most unordered SELECTs follow storage scan order, not hash-table order, and the real tie-order risk is in the SORT operator. All reach figures come from text matching and are lower bounds, as the survey partly admits. The report can use this survey's operator and resolver tables and its coverage-run proposal, after applying the corrections above. It should not use the survey's weighting of which output-order constraints bind a port. It should also add the runner's retry and shared-instance behavior, the debug-sync dependencies, and the storage-estimation coupling before sizing a 'build the judge first' step.

survey.what_it_is: This area measures how long the compiler takes to judge the code. It covers the measured C++ clean and incremental build times on this machine, the CI compile and mysqltest times, the current Rust crate's check and build times, and published or public-CI numbers from large Rust codebases. From these it derives an estimate of cargo check and build time for about 1.83M lines as one crate versus 12-40 crates.

Rust (git ls-files rust): 30 files, 9,216 lines. Of these, 8,448 lines of hand-written .rs (8,420 in src/ plus 28 in build.rs, 272,242 bytes). 534 lines are generated: rust/sql-nio/include/nio.h is cbindgen output that is committed, and CI checks it with git diff. survey.summary:
1. The separate timing build had finished, not still running, by 11:40 (timings.txt ends with DONE). A clean C++ build (build.sh release --make: RelWithDebInfo, -O2 -g, Unity batch 30, lld, no ccache) took 314 s on this Apple M4 Pro (14 cores, 24 GiB). That is about 8 s of configure and about 306 s of make, roughly 7,450 source lines/s, or about 530 lines/s per core.
2. The final lld link takes only about 1.2 s. Per-unit C++ feedback today is 9 s for one standalone .cpp and 37 s for one 27-file, 46,590-line unity group (32 s compile, 3.5 s archive, 1.2 s link).
3. The build log has no per-group timings. The build ends on the src/sql rewrite, resolver and optimizer unity groups.
4. In CI (32 nproc, ccache), the Compile step median is 223 s over 19 runs. A true cold cache (0.32% hit) gives make=556 s plus 258 s dependency init. Warm runs are 116-304 s.
5. The four mysqltest slices have median run times of 574, 374, 447 and 370 s, about 29 min of serial test time for the 272 configured cases. Median wall time for a successful run is about 19 min.
6. The Rust sql-nio crate (8,448 lines) checks in 1.2 s or less on its own, which is at least 7,000 lines/s. Its release build takes 10.3 s or less with lto=thin and codegen-units=1, which is at least about 820 lines/s. Its Cargo.lock is gitignored, so each clean CMake build re-resolves 107 packages.
7. Published numbers for large Rust codebases are thin. TiKV reported 15 min dev and 30 min release rebuilds in 2020 for about 2M lines including dependencies. RisingWave reported 2-3 min debug builds on an M1 in 2023. Feldera measured about 25 min release for 100K lines in one crate, against 2m10s with 1,106 crates. Bun published no build times for its ~780K lines in ~100 crates. Public CI shows 7-15 min checks or clippy runs for TiKV and GreptimeDB (~0.8-1.0M own lines on 3-4 vCPU runners).
8. On stable Rust the parallel frontend is still not available (nightly -Zthreads only, compiler-team#1005, June 2026), so each crate is type-checked on one thread.
9. Scaling assumption: about 3,000 lines/s per M4 Pro core for cargo check of own code (range 1,500-7,000). On that basis one 1.83M-line crate needs about 10 min for a clean check (4-20 min). Its release build with the current codegen-units=1 profile would take about 37 min or more, against the C++ baseline of 5.2 min.
10. With 12-40 balanced crates, a whole-workspace check takes about 2-4 min, and a per-crate check takes about 51 s (12 crates) or about 15 s (40 crates).
11. A per-unit cargo check under 60 s is plausible only if no crate is larger than about 90-180K lines. That means src/sql and src/storage must each be split into several acyclic crates. Only under that condition can Step 4 fold into Step 3; with one 1.83M-line crate, Step 4 remains a separate, batched step.

claims.claim: Estimate for 12-40 balanced crates on 14 cores. A clean workspace check has a floor of about 44 s (610 core-seconds / 14) and is bounded by the dependency chain: about 254 s for 12 crates of about 152K lines over a 5-level chain, and about 122 s for 40 crates of about 46K lines over an 8-level chain. A per-unit check of one crate with upstream crates already checked takes about 51 s for 12 crates (22-102 s) and about 15 s for 40 crates (7-31 s).
claims.evidence: Computed from C17. The chain depths of 5 and 8 levels (oblib -> share -> storage -> sql -> server layering) are an assumption that the coupling area has to confirm.

claims.claim: A per-unit cargo check under 60 s needs every crate to stay under about 180K lines at the central rate: about 90K at the pessimistic rate and 420K at the optimistic one. In balanced crates that is at least 11, 21 or 5 crates respectively. src/sql alone is 983,706 C++ lines, and src/storage is 484,206 lines once the dictionary is excluded, so each must be split into several crates. One 1.83M-line crate cannot meet the budget.
claims.evidence: 60 s times 3,000, 1,500 and 7,000 lines/s. The directory sizes come from the measured size facts in the task (src/sql 983,706 and src/storage 760,249 minus ob_ik_dic.cpp 276,043).

claims.claim: Build-model pain in C++ that Rust modules would remove: unity grouping hides missing #includes until someone builds without unity. At least three commits exist only to repair non-unity builds, and 22b7c24db (#932) alone adds 167 #include lines.
claims.evidence: git log --since=2025-09-28 -i --grep=unity lists 22b7c24db 'Fix compilation in non-unity build (#932)', e45b8ae5c 'fix compile in non-unity' and 6f213cece 'fix compilation errors without unity build'. git show 22b7c24db | grep -c '^+#include' = 167.

claims.claim: Pain in C++ template compile cost that Rust would not remove, since generics monomorphize per crate and Rust has no extern-template equivalent. Commit e2b7c7a8f cut an encoding unity group from 455 s to 53 s and a cs_encoding group from 342 s to 190 s with extern template and ALONE splits; those files were later deleted in cbcea2b91. 27 tracked .cpp files exist only to spread instantiations across compile jobs, and 53c8c5423 split the Boost.Geometry ob_geo_func_*.cpp files for compile time.
claims.evidence: git show e2b7c7a8f (commit message). git log --diff-filter=D for ob_vector_decode_util.h finds cbcea2b91. git ls-files 'src/*' filtered for *_compilation_N / *_compile/*part*.cpp = 27 files in src/share/datum/ob_datum_funcs_compilation (8), ob_str_datum_funcs_compilation (3), src/sql/engine/expr/ob_expr_cmp_func_compile (8) and ob_expr_str_cmp_func_compile (8). The geo split is from git log --grep; 5 files under src/share/geo include boost/geometry.

survey.structure_call:
This area has no code to translate, but it rules out copying the build graph one-to-one. The C++ build uses unity-grouped object targets that are linked together, so dependency cycles between directories cost nothing at link time, and a leaf edit comes back in 9-37 s. Rust makes the crate both the unit of compilation and the unit of type-checking. That crate must sit in an acyclic graph, and on stable Rust its frontend runs on one thread. To keep a per-unit check near today's C++ cost, the Rust layout has to be designed around a crate-size budget of about 90-180K lines, which means at least roughly 20 crates, with src/sql and src/storage each broken up. The release profile also has to change from codegen-units=1. Both are redesign decisions, not translation.

Files that force the call: src/sql (983,706 lines) and src/storage (484,206 non-dictionary lines) are larger than the per-crate budget, and rust/Cargo.toml [profile.release] codegen-units=1 / lto=thin does not scale past one small crate.
hard_parts: The type-checker cost of a single giant crate: stable rustc 1.98.1 (rust/rust-toolchain.toml) runs the frontend serially, and -Zthreads is nightly-only (compiler-team#1005). One 1.83M-line crate needs an estimated 4-20 min per clean check, and incremental check time on a crate that size is unmeasured.

Breaking directory cycles into an acyclic crate graph. Bun needed about 100 crates and hit about 16,000 errors, mostly from untangling cycles. seekdb's C++ targets (ob_sql, ob_share, ob_storage, ob_server, merged into oceanbase_static; see noop.log) do not have to be acyclic today.

Template-heavy code whose C++ compile cost is already managed by hand: extern template and ALONE TUs (commit e2b7c7a8f: 455 s -> 53 s), and the 27 split instantiation files in src/share/datum/ob_datum_funcs_compilation/, src/share/datum/ob_str_datum_funcs_compilation/, src/sql/engine/expr/ob_expr_cmp_func_compile/ and src/sql/engine/expr/ob_expr_str_cmp_func_compile/. Rust generics monomorphize in each crate that uses them, and release builds do not share generics by default. The same slow spots will come back and must be handled through crate boundaries or dyn dispatch.

Boost.Geometry code in src/share/geo (5 files include boost/geometry; objects such as ob_geo_func_symdifference2.cpp.o are 55 MB) has no drop-in Rust equivalent, and it is already a compile-time hotspot (commit 53c8c5423 split it).

The release profile in rust/Cargo.toml (codegen-units=1, lto=thin, debug=true) serializes LLVM for each crate. Applied to a large crate, that is Feldera's failure mode (about 25 min for 100K lines in one crate).

The unity-group reference point is 32 s for 46,590 lines (optimizer_0), which is roughly 1,450 lines/s. A Rust crate of the same size must check in a comparable time for the per-unit loop to stay as fast as C++ today.

Build reproducibility while C++ and Rust are linked together: Cargo.lock is gitignored (rust/.gitignore:5), and cmake/Rust.cmake calls cargo without --locked, so each clean build re-resolves 107 packages. The make-driven cargo call also warns that it could not connect to make's jobserver (full-build.log line 89), which can oversubscribe cores during mixed builds.
pain_instances: 22b7c24db (#932) 'Fix compilation in non-unity build' adds 167 missing #include lines hidden by unity grouping. The same class is fixed in e45b8ae5c ('fix compile in non-unity', 253 files) and 6f213cece ('fix compilation errors without unity build'). Rust modules with explicit use paths remove this class.

The unity-build machinery in cmake/Utils.cmake (UNITY_GROUP assignment, SKIP_UNITY_BUILD_INCLUSION, UNITY_BUILD_CODE_AFTER_INCLUDE at lines 38-129) and cmake/Env.cmake:40 (OB_MAX_UNITY_BATCH_SIZE 30) exists only to make C++ compile times tolerable. Cargo's crate model would replace it.

This one is not removed by Rust, so it is listed as a caution rather than a case for Rust: e2b7c7a8f (455 s unity straggler from duplicate template instantiation) and 53c8c5423 (geo files split for compile time) show that compile-time hotspots come from generic code, and Rust monomorphization has the same cost.
survey.public_surface_tests: Not applicable for compile price as such. As a verification cost: CI runs 272 configured mysqltest cases from tools/deploy/mysqltest_config.yaml (runtime_configs.psmall.test-set), out of 283 tracked .test files under tools/deploy/mysql_test. These are public-surface tests that drive the seekdb binary through obclient/mysqltest (.github/script/seekdb/mysqltest_for_seekdb.py). By suite: 93 top-level, geometry 39, vector_index 21, fork_table 16, fts_index 15, expr 11, subquery 11, type_date 10, global_index 7, datatype 6, and others. One full pass costs about 1,765 s of serial test time on CI runners (4 slices, medians 574/373/447/370 s). Every Step-5 run of a Rust build pays this on top of compile time. Measured from 10 successful seekdb.yml runs.
survey.units_of_work: For the compile referee, the natural unit is the Rust crate, because it is the smallest thing cargo check can judge on its own. Budget: no more than about 180K lines per crate at the central estimate (about 90K pessimistic) to keep a per-unit check under 60 s. For about 1.83M lines that means at least 11 balanced crates at the central rate and at least 21 at the pessimistic rate. With today's uneven directory sizes (src/sql 983,706 lines), about 20-40 crates is realistic, with src/sql and src/storage each split into several crates. C++ units that exist today and can seed the split: 41 CMake targets, 20 BUILD.bazel packages under src, and 364 compile commands (221 unity groups of up to 30 files each, plus 143 standalone TUs).
open_questions: What is the real cargo check throughput, full and incremental, on translated seekdb code, which may be more generic-heavy than sql-nio? This needs a timed pilot of about 50-150K lines in one crate, which I could not run read-only.
How much memory does rustc need to check or build a single 1.83M-line crate, and does it fit in this machine's 24 GiB?
How long does an incremental cargo check take after a one-file edit in a very large crate? rustc re-runs expansion and name resolution over the whole crate, so the cost is unmeasured.

Can src/sql, src/storage and src/share be cut into an acyclic DAG of 20-40 crates, and how deep would the chain be? The coupling area has to answer this; my 5-level and 8-level chain depths are assumptions.
Which C++ unity groups are slowest? This needs a build with timestamps or -ftime-trace, and I did not start one.

What cache state and CPU count did the reference CI numbers use? GitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest (4 vCPU) and macos-15 arm64 (3 vCPU) are assumed from GitHub docs, not verified here, and the cache hit state of the TiKV and Databend jobs is unknown.
When will the rustc parallel frontend reach stable? compiler-team#1005 has a plan but no date.
Does `cargo test --locked -p sql-nio` in .github/workflows/buildbase/action.yml:23 depend on the CMake build first generating the untracked rust/Cargo.lock?
Bun has not published cargo build or check times for its ~780K lines in ~100 crates, so the closest recent agent-driven port has no referee price on record.

checks.corrected: The 3,000 lines/s-per-core central rate has no solid support, and the lower-end derivation is wrong. With the corrected public numbers: TiKV clippy with warm deps checks about 0.73M lines (all-targets) in about 95 s on 3 M1 vCPUs, roughly 2,500-3,800 lines/s per vCPU. GreptimeDB with warm deps checks about 1.0M lines (all-targets) in 425-886 s on 4 x86 vCPUs, roughly 300-900 lines/s per vCPU. The public evidence spans about 5-10x depending on code style, so the rate range should be roughly 500-5,000 lines/s per M4 core, not 1,500-7,000. The serial frontend within a crate and the lack of check pipelining are correctly stated.

checks.corrected: From C17, a clean check of one 1.83M-line crate is about 610 s at 3,000 lines/s, but the plausible range is about 6-60 min (500-5,000 lines/s). Incremental check time is unknown. The release estimate should not rest on sql-nio's '≥818 lines/s': that is a floor on a rate dominated by dependency codegen and LTO, so 1.83M/818 = 2,237 s is an upper bound under that assumption, not the '37 min or more' lower bound stated. Better evidence of release cost under codegen-units=1 and thin LTO comes from Databend (30m37s with 99% sccache hits, driven by one ~181K-line crate plus the link) and Feldera (25 min for 100K lines in one crate). Both point to hours for a single 1.83M-line crate with the current profile.
checks.note: The arithmetic 1.83M/3,000, /7,000, /1,500 and /818 is correct. The direction of the release bound is inverted relative to the evidence.

checks.corrected: The arithmetic is right: a floor of about 44 s, about 254 s for a 5-level chain of 12 crates of ~152K lines, about 122 s for an 8-level chain of 40 crates of ~46K lines, and a per-crate check of about 51 s or about 15 s. But the per-crate figure is the best case: editing a leaf crate, or checking crate N while nothing downstream exists yet, as in bottom-up Step-3 translation. Once downstream crates exist, editing a foundation crate (oblib/share equivalents) re-checks every dependent crate, so the loop costs close to the chain time (about 2-4 min, more at pessimistic rates). The Materialize post attributes its gains exactly to avoiding that invalidation. The 5-level and 8-level depths remain unverified assumptions.

verification.structure_call_check: I agree with the direction: a Rust layout has to be a planned, acyclic set of crates, not a one-to-one copy of the CMake targets, and codegen-units=1 with thin LTO in rust/Cargo.toml cannot stay for large crates. Databend's release build (30m37s with 99% sccache hits, driven by a ~181K-line crate built with codegen-units=1) supports that more strongly than the evidence the survey cites. I disagree with how precise the budget is and with parts of the reasoning. (1) The 90-180K-line-per-crate budget depends on a check rate whose lower-end evidence was misread (TiKV's clippy took ~95 s, not 415 s) and whose other data point was misclassified (GreptimeDB's deps were warm). The honest range is roughly 30-250K lines per crate, i.e. about 8-60 crates. (2) The per-unit estimate ignores downstream re-checks after edits to foundation crates, and those are the common case when fixing shared types in oblib and share. (3) The claim that seekdb 'does not have to be acyclic today' misses that the maintained Bazel build already has an acyclic, analysis-time-validated header-level graph: src/oblib/BUILD.bazel, src/sql/sql_runtime_group_deps.bzl, src/sql/sql_runtime_group_oblib_deps.bzl, src/storage/storage_runtime_group_oblib_deps.bzl, and tools/bazel_migration/generate_oblib_group_deps.py. It has 79 oblib and 116 share interface targets. It stops at headers, and final link cycles are still allowed through seekdb_final_link, but it is the natural starting point for crate boundaries, much better than 41 CMake targets or '20 packages'. (4) The C++ template-cost cautions (e2b7c7a8f, the 27 split files) apply to cargo build, not cargo check, so they bear on Step 5 build time, not on whether Step 4 can fold into Step 3.

verification.overall: The local measurements can be trusted. I re-derived the 314 s clean build, the 1/9/37 s incremental times, the ~1.2 s link, the 364-command and 2.28M-line inventory, and every CI duration and mysqltest statistic from the raw files and gh api, and they match to within rounding. The mysqltest and CI numbers are solid inputs for the report. The weak part is the step from these numbers to the Rust scaling. Two of the three public anchors for the check-rate assumption were misread: TiKV's 415 s was mostly cargo-deny setup (the clippy itself took ~95 s), and GreptimeDB's deps were warm, not cold. The sql-nio release 'rate' is dominated by dependency codegen and LTO, so the 37 min single-crate release figure has its bound pointing the wrong way. The per-unit check estimate also leaves out downstream re-checks. The qualitative conclusion holds: one 1.83M-line crate is too large for a sub-60 s per-unit check, and codegen-units=1 must go. The specific numbers do not: 3,000 lines/s, 90-180K lines per crate, ~20 crates, and the 51/15 s per-crate checks should be read as uncertain by about 5x, with the downside wider than the survey states. They need the pilot the survey itself asks for. The survey also overlooked the Bazel build's existing acyclic header-level target graph and the second cargo build (jemalloc) already in the baseline, and both bear on the crate-split decision.

survey.summary:
1. The ledger covers 6,690 tracked code files (2,804,701 lines, about 28.2M tokens at 3.5 bytes per token) under src/ and rust/. They are assigned to 52 unit groups by directory prefix, and each of the 328 code directories lands in exactly one group. This removes the double counting of share/geo, observer/vector_index, the storage retrieval/vector code and the two cast files.
2. Only 6,468 files, 2,314,419 lines and 24.3M tokens are hand-written. The rest is data (343K lines, 80% of it the one IK dictionary file), generated-and-checked-in code (86.9K lines from five generator families), vendored C (29.4K lines, mostly zstd 1.3.8) and dead files (103 files, 30.9K lines).
3. Several C++ outputs are generated at build time and are not in git: the inner-table schema from a 14,510-line Python definition, three bison/flex parsers, the system-package source and type_name.c. A Rust port has to point these generators at Rust output rather than translate what they produce.
4. The natural unit of work is the stem (.h + .cpp + .ipp with the same base name). There are 3,692 hand-written stems with a median of 2.6K tokens. The sizes are very uneven: about 129 stems over 30K tokens hold a third of all hand-written tokens, and 18 are over 100K.
5. 67 files have 4K lines or more (18 have 8K or more); 54 of them are hand-written, holding 397K lines and 4.57M tokens. Almost every one is a single large class per file (ObDDLService has 381 methods over 23,242 lines), so each splits along method-name families into several `impl` blocks. The two cast files are different: they are matrices of hundreds of free or macro-generated functions and split by source type.
6. Context cost: the direct project headers a stem includes (one level, following forwarding headers) are a median of 25.6K tokens, against 2.6K for the stem itself. Summed over all stems that is 129M tokens, 5.3 times the code; the 30-stem sample gives 7.1 times.
7. The full transitive include closure of a typical stem is a median of 2.4M tokens across about 700 files. A translator can never see all of it and needs summaries of the declarations it does not see.
8. The include graph is tightly coupled: 27 header include cycles covering 69 files, 118 forwarding headers left behind by the Bazel split, and a few headers included by hundreds of files (share/rc/ob_server_runtime.h by 499).
9. Most of the 13 unowned directories (45,854 lines) are thinly tested by mysqltest. sql/tablelock and rootserver/dbms_job have zero active test statements, and change_stream and dbms_scheduler have one test each, while sql/engine/cmd runs in almost every test.
10. Internal unit tests are gone at HEAD: unittest/ holds only .gitignore files, and commit 45cbbe9e1 deleted 678 files there. The 792 mysqltest files are therefore the whole regression base for verifying a migration.

survey.structure_call:
The ledger supports structure-preserving translation at the stem level for most of the code: 3,692 hand-written stems, median 2.6K tokens, each mapping to one Rust module, with class hierarchies kept as they are. Three kinds of files force something other than one-to-one translation.
(a) Build-time and checked-in generators must be pointed at Rust output, not translated. This covers the inner-table schema (14.5K-line Python definition), system variables, error codes, codec SIMD bit-packing and protobuf, about 105K lines of output.
(b) The three bison/flex grammars (sql_parser_mysql_mode.y alone is 18,723 lines and 758 rules with C actions) have no bison-compatible Rust target. They need either a redesign onto another parser generator or keeping the C parser behind FFI.
(c) 54 hand-written files of 4K lines or more must be split before one implementer call can hold them. The single-class files split cleanly into several `impl` blocks by method family; the two cast matrices split by source type and are better produced by a macro or generator.
Data files (IK dictionary, timezone table) and vendored C (zstd, xxhash, libeasy) should be converted by script or replaced with crates. Because a stem's full include closure is a median of 2.4M tokens across about 700 files, a translator can only work from summaries of the declarations it does not see. Header cycles (69 files) set the minimum crate boundaries.
Files that force the call: src/sql/parser/sql_parser_mysql_mode.y, src/pl/parser/pl_parser_mysql_mode.y, src/share/inner_table/ob_inner_table_schema_def.py, src/share/system_variable/gen_ob_sys_variables.py, src/share/gen_errno.pl, src/oblib/lib/codec/generate_simd_bitpakcing.py, src/share/object/ob_obj_cast.cpp, src/sql/engine/expr/ob_datum_cast.cpp, src/rootserver/ob_ddl_service.cpp, src/storage/multi_data_source/mds_node.h.
hard_parts: Single-class files far above one call's size. src/rootserver/ob_ddl_service.cpp (ObDDLService: 381 methods, 23,242 lines, 351K tokens), src/sql/optimizer/ob_join_order.cpp (ObJoinOrder: 286 methods, 14,976 lines), src/sql/rewrite/ob_transform_utils.cpp (368 methods) and src/sql/optimizer/ob_log_plan.cpp (298 methods) must be split into several impl blocks. Their shared member state has to be settled once, before the pieces are translated in parallel.

Cast function matrices produced by macros. src/sql/engine/expr/ob_datum_cast.cpp has 359 CAST_FUNC_NAME(intype,outtype) functions and the OB_DATUM_CAST_MYSQL_IMPLICIT[ObMaxTC][ObMaxTC] table at line 11498. src/share/object/ob_obj_cast.cpp has 413 free functions and OB_OBJ_CAST at line 10086. Both need macro_rules! or a generator plus a const table, not per-function translation.

Bison/flex grammars with C actions: src/sql/parser/sql_parser_mysql_mode.y (18,723 lines, 758 rules, 197 of them opt_* rules) with sql_parser_mysql_mode.l, src/pl/parser/pl_parser_mysql_mode.y/.l, and src/sql/parser/ftsparser.y. Their generated .c output is not in git and has no drop-in Rust generator.

Generators that emit C++ must be rewritten to emit Rust: src/share/inner_table/generate_inner_table_schema.py (3,417 lines) driven by ob_inner_table_schema_def.py (14,510), src/share/system_variable/gen_ob_sys_variables.py (8 output files), src/share/gen_errno.pl (3 outputs from ob_errno.def), src/share/inner_table/sys_package/syspack_codegen.py, and src/share/datum/ob_str_datum_funcs_compilation/gen_str_datum_func_parts.py.

Generated SIMD code: src/oblib/lib/codec/ob_generated_unalign_simd_bp_func.cpp (12,705 lines) together with ob_sse_to_neon.h, built with -mavx2 -mssse3 (src/oblib/lib/CMakeLists.txt:12-19). This maps to std::arch intrinsics with per-arch cfg, or to a regenerated Rust generator.

Header include cycles held together by include guards and forward declarations: 27 cycles covering 69 files, the largest being src/storage/multi_data_source/{mds_node.h, mds_node.ipp, mds_ctx.h, mds_table_base.h, compile_utility/mds_register.h, ...} with src/storage/tx/ob_multi_data_source.h, and 7 files in src/sql/pl (ob_pl.h, pl_cache/ob_pl_cache.h, ...). These files must share one crate.

Template bodies in .ipp files: 40 hand-written .ipp files (22,582 lines), for example src/storage/multi_data_source/mds_node.ipp and src/share/parameter/ob_parameter_seed.ipp (a config definition list). Rust generics and trait bounds must be written out where C++ templates relied on duck typing.

Dense include graph: a stem's transitive closure is a median of 2.41M tokens (108-1,129 files). src/share/rc/ob_server_runtime.h has 499 includers and src/oblib/lib/ob_define.h has 266 includers (23K tokens). Per-unit prompts therefore need a generated declaration index instead of raw headers.

Data compiled as code: src/storage/fts/dict/ob_ik_dic.cpp (276,043 lines, 5.3 MB) and src/oblib/common/timezone/ob_timezone_info.cpp (a 39K-line table with about 1K lines of code after line 38,990). The code must be split out and the tables converted by script, for example to include_bytes! or generated statics.

Vendored C to replace rather than translate: src/oblib/lib/compress/zstd_1_3_8/zstd_src (47 files, 25,154 lines), src/oblib/easy (libeasy with libev's ev.h), and src/oblib/lib/hash_func/xxhash.c. The zstd 1.3.8 on-disk format and version pinning must match whatever crate replaces it.
pain_instances: src/share/gen_errno.pl:268-274 makes the generated ob_errno.cpp keep `#include <iostream>` as a workaround: 'ob_error.cpp file requires at least 20g memory for release(-O2) compilation and will jam when asan turned on ... it is clang bug'. A Rust const table of error codes would not carry this compiler workaround (assessment, not tested).

Template instantiation is sharded by hand across files to spread the compile load: src/share/datum/ob_datum_funcs_compilation/ (8 shard .cpp files plus an .ipp) and src/share/datum/ob_str_datum_funcs_compilation/ (3 shards produced by gen_str_datum_func_parts.py). Rust's codegen-units split a crate automatically, so shard files would not be needed; the compile cost itself remains.

A .cpp file is textually included through headers: src/storage/memtable/mvcc/ob_keybtree.cpp. src/storage/BUILD.bazel:57-60 says 'This .cpp is textually included through the current external Storage header closure' and needs its own _textual_ob_keybtree target. Rust modules have no textual inclusion.

Include-path aliasing: src/CMakeLists.txt:14-19 keeps three include roots so that 'share/inner_table/...', 'inner_table/...' and bare basename spellings of the same generated headers all resolve. There are also 118 forwarding headers (e.g. src/sql/engine/expr/ob_expr_operator.h) that exist only to keep old include spellings. Rust module paths are unique, and a `pub use` replaces a forwarding header.

Commented-out includes leave whole headers dead without any warning. src/storage/tx/ob_trans_factory.h:23 has `// #include "ob_trans_log.h"`, and ob_trans_log.h (412 lines) is included nowhere else. rustc warns about unused items inside the module tree, though not about files outside it (assessment).
survey.public_surface_tests:
The regression base is 792 .test files (283 in tools/deploy/mysql_test, 509 in tools/obtest). At HEAD there are no internal unit tests: unittest/ holds only .gitignore files after 45cbbe9e1 deleted 678 files, and only 2 small tests remain in deps/oblib/unittest. Nothing is left that imports internals. Keyword counts over the 792 files: CREATE TABLE in 666, SET in 451, ALTER SYSTEM in 520, EXPLAIN in 55-65 (depending on pattern), FULLTEXT in 33, MATCH...AGAINST in 12, vector syntax in about 30, ai_* functions or dbms_ai_service in 9 (5 in test_suite/ai_function), GRANT/REVOKE/CREATE USER in 21, LOAD DATA in 1.
Coverage of the unowned directories, with each directory's group:
- sql/engine/cmd (18,401 lines; executors for CREATE/ALTER/DROP, index, user/role/grant, SET, ALTER SYSTEM, LOAD DATA, KILL, vector index refresh, routines) goes to sql-cmd-exec. It runs in nearly every test (CREATE TABLE 666, SET 451, ALTER SYSTEM 520; LOAD DATA only 1).
- sql/monitor (5,534; plan records used by sql/engine/ob_physical_plan.cpp and printer/ob_dml_stmt_printer.cpp, SQL stat records, show trace) goes to sql-core-monitor-printer. Covered through EXPLAIN in about 55-65 tests; SHOW TRACE in 0.
- sql/privilege_check (2,081; privilege checks for every statement and for AI models) goes to sql-cmd-exec. Covered indirectly by all tests; explicit GRANT/REVOKE/CREATE USER in 21.
- sql/executor (1,912; ObCmdExecutor dispatch, execute result, dependency maintenance task) goes to sql-cmd-exec. Covered indirectly by every DDL test.
- sql/tablelock (1,257; LOCK TABLES and GET_LOCK-family executors) goes to sql-cmd-exec. 0 active tests; all matches are commented out in func_group_7.test and yonyou.test.
- observer/change_stream (4,613; reads redo rows and passes them to plugins; the only plugin maintains async vector indexes) goes to search-vector-retrieval. 1 test (vector_index/create_table_with_hybrid_vector_index.test, SYNC_MODE=ASYNC).
- observer/dbms_scheduler (2,890; DBMS_SCHEDULER job master, executor and table operator) goes to jobs-scheduler. 1 test (histogram/stats_farm.test:47-51 calls dbms_scheduler.disable/enable).

- rootserver/dbms_job (1,425; DBMS_JOB master, executor and utils) goes to jobs-scheduler. 0 tests.
- share/text_analysis (839; token stream and analyzer behind the 'space' parser, which is the default per src/oblib/lib/ob_define.h:1444, and the 'beng' parser) goes to fts. Covered by the 33 FULLTEXT tests.
- sql/engine/expr/ob_expr_ai (4,163), observer/ai_service (755) and share/ai_service (479) together form ai-functions (5,397 lines; AI_COMPLETE/EMBED/RERANK/PROMPT, the model-endpoint HTTP client, AI model metadata). 9 tests.
